intro: Minneapolis hides its oldest tree in plain thick woods and puts its oddest one under a bridge. The Rockwood Oak, a bur oak pushing 300 years and a likely candidate for the city's oldest living thing, took a direct hit from the 2011 tornado and is still standing at Theodore Wirth Park. Nearby, students have spent three decades throwing shoes into a plain hackberry for no agreed reason. Add the state's champion basswood and an endangered hemlock planted by a garden's own founder, and four unfamous trees make the case.
meta_description: A tornado-scarred 300-year oak, a hackberry hung with shoes since the 1990s, and Minnesota's champion basswood: 4 remarkable trees around Minneapolis.
question_meta: Minneapolis's likely oldest tree is the Rockwood Oak, a bur oak in Theodore Wirth Park estimated at roughly 300 to 315 years.
question_answer: Minneapolis's likely oldest tree is the Rockwood Oak, a bur oak in Theodore Wirth Regional Park estimated at 300 to 315 years old by the Minneapolis Parks Foundation and Mpls.St.Paul Magazine. It grows in thick woods on the western shore of Wirth Lake and survived a direct hit from the 2011 north Minneapolis tornado.
question_context: Nobody has cored the Rockwood Oak or published a girth figure for it, so the age is an estimate rather than a measurement, and the two sources that offer one differ slightly: the Minneapolis Parks Foundation says 315 years, Mpls.St.Paul Magazine says approximately 300. Both call it a candidate for the city's oldest living thing rather than stating it outright, because nobody has surveyed every old tree in Minneapolis to settle the claim. What makes the age plausible is the species: bur oak is the tree of the prairie edge, with bark thick enough to survive the fires that once ran through Minnesota's oak savanna every few years, which is why the region's oldest trees tend to be bur oaks rather than something thinner-barked. This one had already been growing for a century before Fort Snelling was built downstream, and it carries burls, the lumpy growths that mark a long history on a trunk. It sits off the trail on the western shore of Wirth Lake and takes some looking to find.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Likely the Rockwood Oak, a bur oak in Theodore Wirth Regional Park estimated at 300 to 315 years old. Nobody has surveyed every old tree in the city to settle the claim outright, but both sources that name it call it a leading candidate.

faq.q: Are Minneapolis's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes, all four stand in public parks with no entry fee: Theodore Wirth Regional Park, Bohemian Flats Park, Windom Park and the Eloise Butler Wildflower Garden, which is free but seasonal and gated.

faq.q: What is the Shoe Tree in Minneapolis?
faq.a: A common hackberry in Bohemian Flats Park, beside the Washington Avenue Bridge on the University of Minnesota's West Bank, that students have been hanging tied-together shoes from since at least 1995, for reasons nobody agrees on.

faq.q: Is the Eloise Butler Hemlock always open?
faq.a: No. The Eloise Butler Wildflower Garden and Bird Sanctuary keeps seasonal hours, open April 15 to October 15, Tuesday to Sunday, and the gate is locked outside that window.

trees.name: The Rockwood Oak

location.address: Western shore of Wirth Lake, Theodore Wirth Regional Park, 1 Theodore Wirth Pkwy

trees.access: Free. Stands in a public regional park, embedded in thick woods on the park's southern end near the lake; a trail runs past it but the tree itself takes some looking to spot.
trees.transport: Theodore Wirth Regional Park, northwest Minneapolis; reachable by Metro Transit bus, no rail stop directly at the park.
trees.story:
The tornado that tore through north Minneapolis in 2011 hit this bur oak and did not finish it. It is still standing, and it may well be the oldest living thing in the city. The Minneapolis Parks Foundation puts it at 315 years; Mpls.St.Paul Magazine says approximately 300. Both of them call it a candidate for the city's oldest tree, which is a claim nobody has been able to settle.

Bur oak is the species that makes that plausible. It is the oak of the prairie edge, with bark thick enough to survive the fires that used to run through the oak savanna every few years, which is why Minnesota's true veterans are bur oaks rather than something more delicate. This one carries burls, the lumpy carbuncle-like growths that show on a trunk with a long history behind it.

It had been growing for a century before Fort Snelling went up at the river junction downstream, and the city came later still. It is named for C.J. Rockwood, who helped expand the park around it; Theodore Wirth Regional Park grew up around the tree rather than the other way round.

Finding it takes patience. It sits in thick woods on the western shore of Wirth Lake, near the southern end of the park, and the trail goes past without announcing it. Nobody has published a girth figure, which is an odd gap for a tree with this claim on it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the burls on the trunk, the lumpy growths that mark its age, on a bur oak. It stands in thick woods on the western shore of Wirth Lake, near the southern end of Theodore Wirth Park, just off the trail.

trees.name: The Shoe Tree

location.address: Bohemian Flats Park, Mississippi Gorge Regional Park, west bank of the Mississippi near the Washington Avenue Bridge

trees.access: Free. Public riverside park beside the Washington Avenue Bridge on the University of Minnesota's West Bank.
trees.transport: University of Minnesota West Bank campus; served by campus and city bus routes and the West Bank light rail station, short walk down to Bohemian Flats.
trees.story:
Nobody agrees on why the shoes go up. University of Minnesota students have been throwing tied-together pairs into the branches of this hackberry since at least 1995, when the Minnesota Daily first wrote about it, and the explanations on offer run from graduation ritual to end-of-exams release to no reason anyone can name. The shoes hang until weather or the park takes them down. More arrive.

It is a common hackberry, and that is the honest description: a plain North American tree with rough corky bark and no claim at all to age or size. Nobody has dated it and nobody has measured it. It is here because it is a landmark, which it unarguably is, with its own Wikipedia page and a University of Minnesota Libraries piece written about it, which is more attention than almost any other tree in this city gets.

It stands in Bohemian Flats Park on the west bank of the Mississippi, directly under the Washington Avenue Bridge, on ground where an immigrant settlement of Bohemian, Slovak and Scandinavian families lived down in the river flats until the city cleared them out. The park kept their name.

Go near the end of a semester if you want to catch the tradition in motion. The rest of the year it is a hackberry wearing what other people left behind.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the shoes, pairs tied together and thrown up into the branches for thirty years. It stands in Bohemian Flats Park on the west bank of the Mississippi, directly under the Washington Avenue Bridge.

trees.name: The Windom Park Basswood

location.address: Windom Park, 2251 NE Hayes St, southwest of the park building

trees.transport: Northeast Minneapolis, Windom Park neighbourhood; served by city bus routes.
trees.story:
The largest American basswood recorded in Minnesota is standing in an ordinary neighbourhood park in Northeast Minneapolis, hanging out over a slope behind the park building, with nothing there to tell you so. The Minneapolis Parks Foundation and Mpls.St.Paul Magazine both name it the state champion of its species, and both note the Park Board's Heritage Tree designation. Neither prints a height or a circumference, which is a strange gap for a tree whose entire claim is size.

Basswood is the American lime, and for a fortnight around the turn of June into July it does something an oak never will. The flowers are small, pale and hanging, the scent carries the width of a park, and bees work a tree this size hard enough that you hear it before you reach it. Beekeepers here set their year by the basswood flow.

The rest of the year it is a broad, heart-leaved shade tree, which is what basswoods were planted for along American streets by the thousand.

Nobody has dated it, and champion status is about size rather than years: basswood grows quickly, so a big one need not be an old one. You will find it southwest of the park building on NE Hayes Street, leaning out over the hillside. If anyone has the measurements, we would like them.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, the largest American basswood recorded in Minnesota, and by heart-shaped leaves on a tree leaning out over a slope. It stands just southwest of the park building in Windom Park, off NE Hayes Street.

best_time.label: late June into early July, when the basswood flowers and the whole crown hums with bees

trees.name: The Eloise Butler Hemlock

location.address: Eloise Butler Wildflower Garden and Bird Sanctuary, near the back gate, Theodore Wirth Park, 1 Theodore Wirth Pkwy

trees.access: Free, no entrance fee, but seasonal and gated: the garden is open April 15 to October 15, Tuesday to Sunday (closed Mondays), roughly 7:30am to 6pm (8pm Thu Apr15-Aug31). Outside the season or hours the gate is locked. Public within those hours.
trees.transport: Theodore Wirth Park, northwest Minneapolis; reachable by Metro Transit bus, no rail stop directly at the park.
trees.story:
Minnesota has perhaps fifty mature eastern hemlocks left, and the largest one in Minneapolis was put in the ground by hand. Eloise Butler planted hemlocks in this grove in September 1911, then 28 more on 28 May 1914. The wildflower garden that carries her name grew up around them.

The species is Endangered in Minnesota, raised from Special Concern in 2013. This is the far western edge of a range that properly belongs to the Appalachians and the Great Lakes forests, and the garden's own historians describe this stand as probably the oldest southernmost one left in the state.

This is the biggest tree in it, on the Minneapolis Heritage Tree List for champion size and named a state co-champion for its species. The figures depend on who held the tape: 75 feet tall and 87 inches round by one account, 80 feet and 84 inches by the garden's own. Either reading describes a hemlock of a size Minnesota does not grow any more.

Its age is reasoning rather than record. Nobody wrote down which planting produced this particular tree, but hemlock is slow, and a trunk this thick cannot be one of the saplings added in 1989. That leaves 1911 or 1914, and an age somewhere around 110 to 115 years.

The garden is free and gated. It opens mid-April to mid-October and closes on Mondays, so this is not a tree you can visit in the snow.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by size: the tallest and thickest-trunked of the six hemlocks standing together near the back gate, an evergreen carrying short flat soft needles.
